short: A letter grade, like AAA or BB, from an independent agency showing how likely a borrower is to pay its debts on time.
kid: Imagine your teacher gives each friend stars for how well they give back borrowed toys. Lots of stars means you can lend to them happily. Few stars means be careful.
detail: A credit rating is an independent opinion, published by a credit rating agency, on a borrower's ability and willingness to pay its debts in full and on time. On the common S&P-style scale, ratings run from AAA (highest safety) through AA, A and BBB, which together make up investment grade, down to BB and below, which is speculative grade, and D for default. Agencies rate issuers, such as a company or a country, and individual instruments, such as a specific bond, so a well-secured bond can be rated above its issuer. Ratings matter because many pension funds and insurers can hold only highly rated paper, and lower ratings mean higher borrowing costs. In India, SEBI-registered agencies such as CRISIL, ICRA and CARE Ratings rate bonds, commercial paper and bank loans. A common confusion: a rating is an opinion on default risk only, not a buy or sell recommendation.
example: Say ABC Ltd's bonds are rated AA and XYZ Ltd's are rated BBB. If investors demand 7.8% from ABC and 9.5% from XYZ, then on a ₹100 crore issue XYZ pays ₹9.5 crore of interest a year against ABC's ₹7.8 crore, ₹1.7 crore more, largely because of its weaker rating.

short: A company that studies borrowers and their debts and publishes credit ratings, such as Moody's, S&P, Fitch, or CRISIL and ICRA in India.
kid: Some grown-ups have the job of checking who gives back what they borrow. They tell everyone, so people know whom to trust with their toys.
detail: A credit rating agency assesses the creditworthiness of borrowers and their debt instruments and publishes ratings on a standard letter scale. Globally, three firms dominate: S&P Global Ratings, Moody's and Fitch. In India, agencies must be registered with and regulated by SEBI; the largest include CRISIL, ICRA, CARE Ratings and India Ratings and Research. Most agencies are paid by the issuer whose debt they rate, the 'issuer-pays' model, which creates a potential conflict of interest. Agencies were heavily criticised after the 2008 crisis for awarding AAA ratings to mortgage securities that later collapsed, and in India after IL&FS, which held high investment-grade ratings until shortly before it defaulted in 2018. Their ratings still matter because regulations, fund mandates and loan pricing lean on them. A common confusion: agencies are not regulators, and a rating is an opinion, not a guarantee of repayment.
example: Say ABC Ltd plans a ₹500 crore bond issue and pays an agency to rate it. If the agency assigns AA rather than A, and the better rating lowers the coupon by 0.5 percentage points, ABC saves ₹500 crore × 0.5% = ₹2.5 crore of interest a year.

short: A credit rating for a national government, showing how likely it is to repay what it borrows on time and in full.
kid: This is like giving a whole town stars for keeping its promises. If the town always gives back what it borrows, it gets lots of stars.
detail: A sovereign credit rating is an agency's opinion on a national government's ability and willingness to service its debt. Agencies weigh growth, deficits and public debt, inflation, external balances, foreign exchange reserves and institutional strength. Separate ratings usually exist for debt in the country's own currency and in foreign currency. The rating matters well beyond the government: it often acts as a ceiling for companies based in that country, and it influences foreign investor flows and borrowing costs across the economy. India sat at the lowest investment-grade notch with all three global agencies for many years until S&P upgraded it to BBB in August 2025; check the agencies' sites for current ratings. In May 2025 Moody's cut the US from Aaa to Aa1. A common confusion: governments rarely default on local-currency debt because, in the last resort, their central bank can create the money; foreign-currency debt carries the bigger risk.
example: Say a country's 10-year bond yields 7.0% and a ratings upgrade brings that down to 6.8%. On ₹10 lakh crore of new borrowing, the 0.2 percentage point saving cuts the government's interest bill by ₹2,000 crore a year.

short: Credit ratings of BBB- (or Baa3) and above, given to borrowers judged fairly likely to repay their debts in full and on time.
kid: When a friend has nearly always given back toys on time, you put them in your 'happy to lend to' group.
detail: Investment grade covers ratings of BBB- or higher on the S&P and Fitch scales, or Baa3 or higher on Moody's scale. Bonds in this band are judged to have adequate to very strong capacity to repay. The cut-off matters enormously because many pension funds, insurers and bank rules restrict holdings to investment-grade paper, and many bond indices include only investment-grade issues. So a borrower that slips below BBB- can face forced selling and a jump in borrowing costs. Indian agencies use the same letter scale, and many Indian investment rules for insurers and debt mutual funds lean heavily on these grades. A common confusion: investment grade does not mean risk-free. A BBB- bond still carries meaningful default risk, far more than a AAA bond, and investment-grade issuers have defaulted, sometimes after being downgraded several notches in a short time.
example: Say ABC Ltd is rated BBB- and pays 8.5% on ₹1,000 crore of bonds, or ₹85 crore a year. If it is cut one notch to BB+ and investors then demand 10%, refinancing the same bonds would cost ₹100 crore a year, ₹15 crore more.

short: A bond rated below investment grade (BB+ or lower), which pays higher interest because its issuer is more likely to default.
kid: If a friend sometimes forgets to give back toys, they might offer you an extra sweet to lend to them anyway. You get more sweets, but you might lose the toy.
detail: A high-yield bond, popularly called a junk bond, carries a rating of BB+ or lower (Ba1 or lower at Moody's). Issuers are typically highly indebted companies, young firms or businesses in difficulty, and they must offer much higher yields than investment-grade borrowers to compensate for greater default risk. The US has a large, liquid high-yield market, built up from the 1980s, that funds many leveraged buyouts. In India the market for corporate bonds rated below AA is thin, so weaker borrowers rely mostly on banks, NBFCs and private credit funds. High-yield bonds behave partly like equities: prices fall sharply in recessions as default fears rise. A common confusion: a high yield is not the same as a high expected return. Defaults and low recoveries can eat up much of the extra interest, so the promised yield is the best case, not the likely outcome.
example: Say a 5-year US Treasury yields 4% and a hypothetical BB-rated company's 5-year bond yields 7%. If 2% of such bonds default each year and investors recover 40%, the expected annual credit loss is 2% × (1 - 0.4) = 1.2%, so the investor's extra return over Treasuries is closer to 3% - 1.2% = 1.8% than to 3%.

short: A company or bond that used to be rated investment grade but has been downgraded below BBB-, into junk territory.
kid: A friend who always shared nicely starts forgetting to give things back. Now people are less sure about lending to them.
detail: A fallen angel is an issuer, or its bonds, originally rated investment grade and later cut to high yield, below BBB- or Baa3. The reverse, a junk issuer upgraded to investment grade, is called a rising star. Fallen angels matter because the downgrade forces many investment-grade-only funds and index trackers to sell, often all at once, while high-yield investors may not be able to absorb the supply quickly. This forced selling can push prices below fair value, which is why some funds deliberately buy fallen angels after the downgrade. A large wave came in early 2020, when the pandemic pushed several big issuers, including Ford Motor at S&P, into junk. A common confusion: becoming a fallen angel does not mean default is imminent. Many are large, established businesses that stay in the BB range and keep paying, and some regain investment grade within a few years.
example: Say a fund holds ₹50 crore face value of ABC Ltd bonds rated BBB-. ABC is cut to BB+ and the price falls from ₹100 to ₹90 per ₹100 of face value as investment-grade funds sell, so the holding drops to ₹45 crore, a ₹5 crore mark-to-market loss.

short: An agency's signal of where a credit rating may head over roughly the next six months to two years: positive, negative or stable.
kid: Your teacher says, 'You have three stars now and you are getting better, so you may get a fourth soon.' That hint tells you what might come next.
detail: A rating outlook accompanies a long-term credit rating and signals its likely direction over the medium term, typically six months to two years. Positive means an upgrade is possible, negative means a downgrade is possible, stable means no change is expected, and developing means it could go either way. An outlook change is not a rating action, and many outlooks are later returned to stable without any change in the rating. Markets still pay attention: a shift to negative can widen credit spreads before any downgrade happens, and upgrades usually follow a period on positive outlook. Sovereign outlooks get heavy coverage in India because they affect foreign investor flows. A common confusion: an outlook is different from a rating watch. A watch is shorter term and means the agency is actively considering a change, usually because of a specific event such as a merger.
example: Say ABC Ltd, with EBITDA of ₹1,000 crore and net debt of ₹2,000 crore, is rated A with a stable outlook. It borrows another ₹2,000 crore to buy back shares, taking net debt to EBITDA from 2x to 4x; the agency keeps the A rating but revises the outlook to negative.

short: A formal notice that an agency is actively considering changing a credit rating soon, usually because of a specific event such as a merger.
kid: Your teacher says, 'Something big just happened, so I am checking your stars again this week.' Everyone waits to see if the stars go up or down.
detail: A rating watch, called CreditWatch at S&P and a review at Moody's, signals that a rating is under active consideration for change in the near term, often within about 90 days. It is triggered by a specific event, such as a large debt-funded acquisition, a regulatory action, a sudden liquidity squeeze or an expected change in government support. A watch has a direction: negative, positive or developing, where the outcome could go either way. Indian agencies use similar labels such as 'rating watch with negative implications'. A watch is a stronger signal than an outlook because the agency is actively deciding and usually resolves it with a rating action. Lenders and investors track watches closely because loan pricing and fund mandates react to rating changes. A common confusion: being placed on watch is not itself a downgrade. The rating stays unchanged until the agency completes its review.
example: Say ABC Ltd, rated AA, announces a ₹5,000 crore acquisition funded entirely with new debt. The agency places it on rating watch with negative implications; two months later, once the deal closes, it cuts the rating one notch to AA- and removes the watch.

short: The chance that someone who owes you money does not pay it back in full or on time, causing you a loss.
kid: When you lend your crayons to a friend, there is a chance they lose some or never give them back. That little worry is what this word is about.
detail: Credit risk is the risk of loss when a borrower, bond issuer or trading counterparty fails to meet its payment obligations. It covers outright default and late payment, and also the fall in a bond's value when the issuer's creditworthiness worsens even without a default, sometimes called downgrade or spread risk. Lenders measure it with probability of default, loss given default and exposure at default, and they price it through higher interest rates or credit spreads. For banks it is usually the largest risk on the balance sheet, which is why regulators such as the RBI require capital and provisions against loans. India's bad-loan cycle of the late 2010s was credit risk playing out on a large scale. A common confusion: credit risk is different from interest rate risk. A government bond has almost no credit risk but can still lose value when interest rates rise.
example: Say a bank lends ₹10 crore to ABC Ltd. If there is a 3% chance ABC defaults and the bank would recover 40% in that case, the expected loss is 0.03 × 60% × ₹10 crore = ₹18 lakh.

short: How likely a borrower is to repay debt in full and on time, judged from its income, existing debts, assets and track record.
kid: Before lending your bike, you think: does this friend take care of things and give them back? If yes, they are someone you can trust.
detail: Creditworthiness is a lender's judgement of whether a borrower can and will repay, and the process of assessing it is called credit appraisal or underwriting. Lenders often use the 'five Cs': character (track record and integrity), capacity (cash flow to service debt), capital (the owner's own money at stake), collateral (assets pledged) and conditions (the economy, the industry and the loan's terms). For companies, analysts study ratios such as net debt to EBITDA, interest coverage and debt service coverage; for individuals in India, lenders also check credit scores from bureaus such as CIBIL. The result decides whether a loan is approved, for how much, at what rate and with which covenants. A common confusion: a profitable company is not automatically creditworthy. Profits can be tied up in unpaid customer bills or inventory, so lenders focus on the cash actually available to repay.
example: Say ABC Ltd earns EBITDA of ₹120 crore and owes ₹80 crore a year in interest plus principal repayments. On this simple EBITDA-based measure its debt service coverage is 120 / 80 = 1.5x, which many lenders find comfortable; below 1.0x, operating cash would not cover repayments.

short: Failing to make a promised debt payment of interest or principal on time, or breaking other key terms of a loan or bond.
kid: You promised to give back your friend's toy car on Friday, but Friday comes and you can't. You broke your promise to give it back.
detail: A default occurs when a borrower misses a scheduled payment of interest or principal beyond any grace period, or breaches another term, such as a covenant, that the agreement treats as an event of default. Once in default, lenders can usually demand immediate repayment, enforce security, or push the borrower into restructuring or insolvency proceedings. In India, under RBI norms as of 2025, a bank loan overdue for more than 90 days becomes a non-performing asset, and rating agencies move rated bonds to 'D' even after a very short delay. Defaults spread: the IL&FS default in 2018 froze funding across much of the NBFC sector. A common confusion: default is not the same as bankruptcy. A firm can default and then restructure or catch up on payments without ever entering formal insolvency, and a covenant breach can be a 'technical default' while every payment is still being made.
example: Say ABC Ltd owes ₹15 crore of interest on its ₹200 crore bonds on 30 June but pays nothing, and the 7-day grace period also lapses. That missed payment is a default, and if the bond terms allow acceleration, bondholders can demand the full ₹200 crore back immediately.

short: A contract-defined trigger, such as bankruptcy or a missed payment, that lets lenders demand repayment or makes credit protection pay out.
kid: You and a friend agree: 'If my kite breaks, you give me yours.' The kite breaking is the special thing that makes the promise happen.
detail: In credit derivatives, a credit event is a trigger defined in standard ISDA documentation that makes a credit default swap pay out. The core events are bankruptcy, failure to pay and, for many contracts, restructuring; obligation acceleration and repudiation or moratorium are also used, especially for sovereigns. Whether an event has happened is decided by ISDA's Credit Derivatives Determinations Committees, made up of major dealers and investors. In loan and bond documents, the related term 'event of default' lists the triggers, such as non-payment, covenant breach, insolvency, cross-default or a material adverse change, that let lenders accelerate repayment. A famous case was Greece in 2012, when its use of collective action clauses to force losses on bondholders was ruled a credit event, triggering CDS payouts. A common confusion: not every distressed situation counts. A purely voluntary debt exchange may not be a credit event at all.
example: Say an investor holds $10 million of CDS protection on a hypothetical company. The company files for bankruptcy, a credit event, and the settlement auction values its bonds at 35% of face value, so the protection seller pays $10 million × (1 - 0.35) = $6.5 million.

short: In India, a borrower who could repay a bank loan but deliberately does not, or who misuses or diverts the borrowed money.
kid: Some friends can't give your toy back because it broke. But one friend still has it and just won't give it back. That friend is being unfair on purpose.
detail: Wilful defaulter is an Indian regulatory classification, set out in RBI directions, for a borrower that defaults despite having the capacity to pay, diverts or siphons off loan money for other purposes, or sells assets pledged to the lender without its consent. Lenders must follow a formal process, including a review committee and a chance for the borrower to respond, before applying the label. The consequences under the rules as of 2025 are severe: the borrower and its promoters are cut off from fresh credit from banks and NBFCs, barred from raising money through public issues under SEBI rules, and disqualified from bidding for companies under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code. Their names are also reported to credit information companies. A common confusion: most defaulters are not wilful. A company that cannot pay because its business collapsed is a defaulter, but not a wilful one.
example: Say ABC Ltd borrows ₹200 crore from a bank to build a factory but moves ₹120 crore of it to an unrelated firm owned by its promoter, then stops repaying. Because the money was diverted, the bank can begin proceedings to classify ABC and its promoters as wilful defaulters.

short: The estimated chance, usually over one year, that a borrower will fail to repay its debt.
kid: If you lend crayons to ten friends and one usually forgets to give them back, the chance of losing your crayons is one in ten.
detail: Probability of default, or PD, is the likelihood that a borrower defaults within a given time horizon, usually one year. It is one of the three building blocks of credit risk measurement, alongside loss given default and exposure at default. Banks estimate PD from internal rating models, historical default rates by rating grade, financial ratios and market signals such as bond spreads and CDS prices; under the Basel internal ratings-based approaches, approved banks use their own PD estimates to set capital. Historical data show PD rises steeply as ratings fall: one-year default rates for AAA companies are close to zero, while single-B issuers default far more often. Expected credit loss provisioning under Ind AS 109 and IFRS 9 also relies on PD. A common confusion: PDs implied by market prices are usually higher than historical default rates, because spreads also pay investors for bearing risk and illiquidity.
example: Say a bank's model gives a group of 500 similar borrowers a one-year PD of 2% each. The bank should expect about 500 × 2% = 10 of them to default over the coming year.
formula: Implied annual PD ≈ Credit spread / (1 - Recovery rate)

short: The share of the money owed that a lender loses if the borrower defaults, after counting whatever it manages to recover.
kid: You lend a friend ten sweets, but they can only give back four. You lost six out of ten. That lost part is what this measures.
detail: Loss given default, or LGD, is the percentage of an exposure a lender expects to lose if a borrower defaults, after recoveries from collateral, guarantees and insolvency proceedings, net of recovery costs. It equals one minus the recovery rate. LGD depends heavily on seniority and security: senior secured loans backed by good collateral usually have low LGDs, while unsecured or subordinated debt can lose most of its value. Banks combine LGD with probability of default and exposure at default to estimate expected loss, set provisions and price loans; under Basel's foundation approach regulators prescribe LGD values, while banks on advanced approaches model their own. In India, slow resolution and low recoveries in many insolvency cases have meant high LGDs on stressed corporate loans. A common confusion: LGD is measured against the amount outstanding at default, not the original loan amount.
example: Say ABC Ltd defaults owing a bank ₹50 crore, and the bank recovers ₹20 crore by selling collateral after spending ₹2 crore on legal costs. Net recovery is ₹18 crore, so LGD = (50 - 18) / 50 = 64%.
formula: LGD = 1 - Recovery rate = (Exposure at default - Net recoveries) / Exposure at default

short: The total amount a borrower owes a lender at the moment it defaults, including credit lines it draws down just before.
kid: Your friend has borrowed three toys and asks for two more just before saying they can't give any back. Now five of your toys are missing, not three.
detail: Exposure at default, or EAD, is the amount a lender is owed when a borrower defaults. For a fully drawn term loan it is roughly the outstanding principal plus accrued interest. For revolving credit lines, overdrafts and credit cards it is harder to estimate, because borrowers in trouble tend to draw down their unused limits just before they default. Banks therefore apply a credit conversion factor to the undrawn portion to estimate how much will be used. EAD is the third input, alongside probability of default and loss given default, in the expected loss formula, and it drives Basel capital requirements. For derivatives, exposure depends on future market moves and is modelled through potential future exposure. A common confusion: EAD is neither the sanctioned limit nor today's balance; it is an estimate of the balance on the future date of default.
example: Say ABC Ltd has a ₹100 crore credit line with ₹40 crore drawn. If the bank assumes distressed borrowers draw 60% of their unused limit, EAD = ₹40 crore + 60% × ₹60 crore = ₹76 crore.
formula: EAD = Drawn amount + Credit conversion factor × Undrawn commitment

short: The average credit loss a lender should expect on a loan or portfolio, calculated as default chance times loss share times amount owed.
kid: If you lend lots of marbles to lots of friends, a few will get lost. Guessing how many you will lose, on average, helps you plan.
detail: Expected loss is the average loss a lender anticipates from credit risk over a period, usually one year, calculated as probability of default times loss given default times exposure at default. Because it is predictable across a large portfolio, banks treat it as a normal cost of lending: they cover it through the interest margin they charge and through provisions. Capital, by contrast, is held against unexpected loss, the extra damage in bad years beyond the average. The idea links directly to accounting: expected credit loss provisioning under IFRS 9 and Ind AS 109, already used by larger Indian NBFCs, builds on the same inputs, and RBI draft rules issued in 2025 propose moving banks onto it as well. A common confusion: expected loss is an average across many loans, not a forecast for any single loan, which will either repay in full or default with a much larger loss.
example: Say a bank lends ₹20 crore to ABC Ltd with a PD of 2%, an LGD of 45% and an EAD of ₹20 crore. Expected loss = 0.02 × 0.45 × ₹20 crore = ₹18 lakh, so the loan's pricing should cover at least 0.9% a year for credit losses.

short: The share of the money owed that lenders get back after a borrower defaults, usually shown as a percentage of the amount due.
kid: A friend lost some of your toys but gives back the ones that are left. The part that comes back to you is what this measures.
detail: The recovery rate is the proportion of a defaulted claim that creditors eventually get back, through collateral sales, a restructuring or insolvency proceedings. It equals one minus loss given default. Recovery depends on seniority, security, the value of the business or its assets, the legal system and how long resolution takes. Global studies typically find that senior secured loans recover much more than senior unsecured bonds, and subordinated debt recovers the least. In credit default swap pricing, the market often assumes a standard 40% recovery for senior unsecured corporate debt. In India, the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code improved recoveries compared with older routes, but as of 2025 average realised recoveries were roughly a third of admitted claims, often after long delays. A common confusion: a quoted recovery rate usually ignores the time value of money, and getting 50% back after four years is worth far less than 50% today.
example: Say ABC Ltd defaults on ₹500 crore of bonds, and two years later bondholders receive ₹175 crore under the resolution plan. The recovery rate is 175 / 500 = 35%, so the loss given default is 65%.
formula: Recovery rate = Amount recovered / Amount owed at default = 1 - LGD

short: The extra yield a risky bond pays over a safe government bond of the same maturity, as compensation for the chance of default.
kid: A friend who sometimes forgets to return things offers you two extra sweets to borrow your toy. A very careful friend offers none. The extra sweets are your reward for taking a chance.
detail: A credit spread is the difference between the yield on a bond with credit risk, such as a corporate bond, and the yield on a comparable risk-free government bond of the same maturity, usually quoted in basis points. It compensates investors for expected default losses, plus extra premiums for uncertainty and lower liquidity. Spreads widen when investors worry about the economy or a particular issuer and tighten when confidence returns, so they are a closely watched gauge of financial stress. In India, corporate bond spreads are measured against government securities of the same tenor. Related measures include the G-spread, the Z-spread and the option-adjusted spread. A common confusion: a wider spread does not automatically make a bond cheap. It may reflect genuinely higher default risk, and spreads can also widen simply because liquidity dries up, with no change in the issuer's health.
example: Say a 5-year AAA bond of ABC Ltd yields 7.6% while a 5-year government security yields 6.9%. The credit spread is 7.6% - 6.9% = 0.7 percentage points, or 70 basis points.
formula: Credit spread = Yield on risky bond - Yield on risk-free bond of the same maturity

short: A contract that works like insurance against a borrower's default: the buyer pays regular fees, and the seller pays out if default happens.
kid: You give a big kid one sweet every week. If your friend ever loses the toy you lent, the big kid buys you a new one.
detail: A credit default swap is a derivative in which the protection buyer pays a periodic premium, the CDS spread, to a protection seller, who in return compensates the buyer for losses if a named reference entity suffers a credit event such as bankruptcy or failure to pay. Settlement usually follows an auction that fixes the defaulted bonds' recovery value. CDS let banks and investors hedge credit risk or take views on creditworthiness without owning the bonds, and CDS spreads serve as a real-time market gauge of default risk for companies and governments. They were central to the 2008 crisis, when AIG had sold vast amounts of protection it could not honour. The RBI permits CDS in India, but the market remains small. A common confusion: unlike insurance, the buyer need not own the underlying bond, and the protection is only as good as the seller's ability to pay.
example: Say an investor buys 5-year CDS protection on $10 million of a hypothetical company's debt at a spread of 200 basis points, paying $10 million × 2% = $200,000 a year. If the company defaults and the auction sets recovery at 30%, the seller pays $10 million × (1 - 0.30) = $7 million.
formula: Annual CDS premium = CDS spread × Notional; Payout on a credit event = Notional × (1 - Recovery rate)

short: A promise written into a loan or bond agreement that the borrower must keep, such as limiting its debt or keeping enough cash flow.
kid: When you lend your bike, you say: 'You can borrow it if you promise not to ride in the mud.' Your friend must keep that promise to keep the bike.
detail: A covenant is a condition in a loan or bond agreement that protects lenders by restricting what the borrower may do or by requiring it to stay financially healthy. Affirmative covenants require actions, such as providing audited accounts or insuring assets. Negative covenants forbid actions, such as taking on more debt, selling key assets or paying large dividends. Financial covenants set numeric tests, for example net debt to EBITDA below 3.5x or interest coverage above 2x, checked every quarter (maintenance covenants) or only when the borrower takes a particular step (incurrence covenants). Breaching a covenant is usually an event of default that lets lenders demand repayment, although in practice they often grant a waiver in return for a fee or a higher interest rate. A common confusion: a covenant breach does not need a missed payment. A company can pay every rupee on time and still be in technical default.
example: Say ABC Ltd's loan requires net debt to EBITDA of no more than 3.5x. With net debt of ₹700 crore and EBITDA of ₹250 crore, the ratio is 700 / 250 = 2.8x. If EBITDA falls to ₹180 crore, it rises to 700 / 180 ≈ 3.9x, breaching the covenant even though every interest payment has been made.

short: A loan with few or no regular financial tests on the borrower, giving lenders less early warning and less power if things go wrong.
kid: You lend your bike and don't make your friend promise anything. That is easier for your friend, but you can't step in if they start riding it badly.
detail: A covenant-lite loan lacks the maintenance financial covenants found in traditional loans, such as quarterly tests of leverage or interest coverage. It usually keeps only incurrence covenants, which are checked only when the borrower takes a specific action such as raising more debt or paying a dividend. Cov-lite structures came to dominate the US and European leveraged loan markets during the 2010s, because heavy demand from CLOs and credit funds gave private equity owners the bargaining power to demand looser terms. For borrowers they mean flexibility; for lenders they remove the early trigger to renegotiate before a company's finances deteriorate badly, and rating agencies have argued this tends to lower recoveries when defaults do happen. Indian bank loans typically still carry maintenance covenants. A common confusion: cov-lite does not mean no covenants at all, and it does not by itself mean the borrower is weak.
example: Say lenders give a hypothetical company a $500 million cov-lite term loan when its EBITDA is $100 million, so leverage is 5x. If EBITDA falls to $60 million, leverage jumps to about 8.3x, yet with no maintenance test the lenders cannot step in as long as interest is paid.

short: The order in which lenders and investors get paid if a company fails; more senior claims are paid back before more junior ones.
kid: When there is only a little cake left, the friends at the front of the line get their slice first. Those at the back might get crumbs or nothing.
detail: Seniority ranks the claims on a company's assets and cash flows if it is liquidated or goes bankrupt. A typical order runs: secured creditors, up to the value of their collateral, then senior unsecured debt, then subordinated debt, then preference shareholders, and finally equity holders, who get whatever is left. The absolute priority rule says each class should be paid in full before the class below receives anything, although negotiated restructurings sometimes deviate from it. Seniority is a major driver of loss given default and therefore of pricing: junior instruments pay higher yields because they are paid last. In India, Section 53 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code sets the liquidation waterfall, with insolvency costs, workmen's dues and secured creditors near the top. A common confusion: seniority is about ranking in a failure, not about which debt is repaid first in normal times; maturity dates decide that.
example: Say ABC Ltd is liquidated for ₹300 crore, net of costs, and owes ₹200 crore to senior secured lenders, ₹150 crore to senior unsecured bondholders and ₹100 crore of subordinated debt. Secured lenders get ₹200 crore in full, unsecured bondholders get the remaining ₹100 crore (about 67% of their claim), and subordinated holders and shareholders get nothing.

short: Debt that ranks first for repayment if a borrower fails, ahead of junior debt and shareholders, so it is safer and pays less interest.
kid: Imagine being first in the line for cake. Even if there is not much cake left, you are likely to get your slice.
detail: Senior debt has the highest repayment priority in a company's capital structure. It is often split into senior secured debt, backed by specific collateral, and senior unsecured debt, which has no specific security but still ranks above subordinated debt. Bank term loans, revolving credit facilities and most investment-grade corporate bonds are senior. Because senior lenders are paid first in a liquidation, their recovery rates are higher and the interest they charge is lower than for junior debt. In leveraged buyouts, senior loans usually form the largest and cheapest slice of the borrowing. A common confusion: senior does not mean secured. A senior unsecured bond ranks behind secured debt to the extent of the collateral's value, so two instruments both labelled 'senior' can have very different recovery prospects in a default.
example: Say a private equity firm buys a hypothetical company for $1.2 billion, funded with $600 million of senior loans at 8%, $200 million of subordinated debt at 12% and $400 million of equity. The senior loans are half the total and cost $48 million a year in interest, against $24 million for the smaller subordinated slice.

short: Debt that is repaid only after senior debt if the borrower fails, so it is riskier and pays a higher interest rate.
kid: Imagine standing near the back of the line for cake. You only get a slice if everyone in front has had theirs and some is left.
detail: Subordinated debt ranks below senior debt in repayment priority, either through a contractual subordination clause or because it is issued by a holding company whose operating subsidiaries owe money to others first. In a liquidation, holders are paid only after senior creditors are repaid in full, though still ahead of preference and equity shareholders. Because recoveries are lower, subordinated debt carries higher yields and usually lower ratings than the same issuer's senior debt. Banks are major issuers, since regulators count certain subordinated instruments as capital; Indian banks issue Basel III Tier 2 bonds and riskier Additional Tier 1 bonds. The 2020 write-down of Yes Bank's AT1 bonds, contested in court for years afterwards, showed how much deeply subordinated bank debt can lose. A common confusion: subordinated does not mean unsafe in normal times. It pays interest like other debt until the issuer gets into trouble.
example: Say ABC Ltd's senior bonds yield 8% and its subordinated bonds 10.5%. An investor putting ₹10 lakh into the subordinated bonds earns ₹1.05 lakh a year, ₹25,000 more than the ₹80,000 from senior bonds, as payment for standing behind senior lenders in a default.

short: A layer of financing between senior debt and equity, usually unsecured and subordinated, that pays high interest and often includes equity-linked rights.
kid: Think of a three-layer cake. The bottom layer is the safest, the top is the riskiest, and the middle layer is a bit risky but comes with extra icing as a reward.
detail: Mezzanine debt sits between senior debt and common equity in the capital structure, so it absorbs losses after equity is wiped out but before senior lenders lose anything. It is typically unsecured or holds only a second-ranking claim on assets, and it usually comes from specialised funds rather than banks. To compensate for that risk it targets high returns, often combining cash interest, payment-in-kind interest that is added to the principal, and equity kickers such as warrants. Companies use it for buyouts, acquisitions or expansion when senior lenders will not lend more and owners want to avoid the dilution of a pure equity raise. In India, structured credit and special situations funds, often set up as alternative investment funds, fill this role. A common confusion: mezzanine is debt in legal form, but its risk and return sit much closer to equity than to a bank loan.
example: Say ABC Ltd raises ₹100 crore of mezzanine debt at 12% cash interest plus 4% payment-in-kind interest. In year one it pays ₹12 crore in cash, while ₹4 crore is added to the principal, so it owes ₹104 crore at the start of year two.

short: Debt backed by specific assets that the lender can take and sell if the borrower fails to repay.
kid: You lend a friend your bike, and they let you keep their skateboard until they bring the bike back. If they don't, you keep the skateboard.
detail: Secured debt is backed by a charge over specific assets, such as property, machinery, receivables or shares, which the lender can enforce if the borrower defaults. Home loans, vehicle loans, most bank term loans to companies and secured non-convertible debentures are common examples. Because the lender has a fallback, secured debt usually carries lower interest rates and higher recovery rates than unsecured debt. In India, banks and other eligible lenders can enforce security on many secured loans under the SARFAESI Act without first going to court, and secured creditors rank near the top of the insolvency waterfall. Lenders also apply a haircut, lending less than the asset's value, to cover a fall in its price. A common confusion: secured does not mean risk-free. If the collateral turns out to be worth less than the debt, the shortfall becomes a weaker unsecured claim, and enforcing security can take years.
example: Say a bank lends ₹60 lakh against a flat valued at ₹80 lakh, a loan-to-value ratio of 60 / 80 = 75%. If the borrower defaults and the flat sells for ₹70 lakh, the bank can recover its ₹60 lakh in full from the sale, with any surplus after interest and costs returned to the borrower.

short: Debt with no specific assets pledged to back it, so the lender relies only on the borrower's promise and general ability to pay.
kid: You lend your friend a toy and keep nothing of theirs in return. You just trust them to bring it back.
detail: Unsecured debt is not backed by a charge on any particular asset. Credit cards, personal loans, commercial paper and most US investment-grade corporate bonds are typical examples. If the borrower defaults, unsecured creditors have a general claim on whatever assets remain, ranking behind secured creditors to the extent of their collateral but ahead of shareholders. Because lenders carry more risk, unsecured debt usually costs more than secured debt for the same borrower. In India, the RBI raised risk weights on unsecured consumer credit, such as personal loans and credit cards, in November 2023 to cool its rapid growth, a sign of how closely regulators watch this segment. A common confusion: unsecured does not mean junior. Senior unsecured bonds still rank above subordinated debt, and a strong company's unsecured bonds can be safer than a weak company's secured loan.
example: Say a bank charges ABC Ltd 9% on a secured term loan and 11% on an unsecured loan of the same size. On ₹50 crore, the unsecured loan costs ₹5.5 crore of interest a year, ₹1 crore more than the ₹4.5 crore on the secured one.

short: An asset a borrower pledges to a lender, which the lender can take and sell if the loan is not repaid.
kid: To borrow your friend's bike, you give them your favourite toy to hold. If you don't bring the bike back, they keep the toy.
detail: Collateral is property pledged to secure a loan, giving the lender a legal claim, called a charge or lien, that it can enforce on default. In Indian lending the form of charge depends on the asset: a mortgage for land and buildings, hypothecation for movable assets such as vehicles, stock or receivables that stay with the borrower, and a pledge where the lender holds the asset, as with shares or gold. Lenders lend less than the collateral's value, applying a haircut or loan-to-value limit, to protect against price falls. Collateral also underpins markets beyond loans: repo deals, derivatives margining and clearing houses all rely on posted collateral. A common confusion: collateral reduces the lender's loss if a borrower defaults, but it does not make default less likely, and its value often falls exactly when defaults rise.
example: Say ABC Ltd pledges shares worth ₹100 crore and the lender, requiring 2x cover, lends ₹50 crore. If the share price falls 30%, the shares are worth ₹70 crore, so the lender asks ABC to pledge another ₹30 crore of shares to restore cover of ₹100 crore.

short: Latin for 'with equal step': creditors who rank equally, sharing any repayments in proportion to their claims, with none ahead of the others.
kid: Two friends each lent you sweets, and you only have a few left. You share them out fairly so each friend gets back the same part of what they lent.
detail: Pari passu, Latin for 'with equal step', means that two or more claims rank equally, so any payments or recoveries are shared pro rata. A pari passu clause in a bond or loan promises that the debt will rank at least equally with the borrower's other debt of the same class, usually its other senior unsecured obligations. In India, banks in a lending consortium often hold a pari passu charge over the same assets and share the sale proceeds in proportion to what each is owed. The clause became famous in Argentina's sovereign debt battle, when US courts from 2012 read it to bar Argentina from paying restructured bondholders unless it also paid holdout creditors. A common confusion: pari passu means equal ranking, not equal amounts. Each creditor receives the same percentage of its claim, not the same rupee sum.
example: Say ABC Ltd owes ₹60 crore to Bank A and ₹40 crore to Bank B under a pari passu charge, and the pledged assets sell for ₹50 crore. Both recover 50 / 100 = 50% of their claims, so Bank A gets ₹30 crore and Bank B gets ₹20 crore.

short: A loan for a fixed amount, repaid with interest over a set period, often used to buy long-lived assets such as machinery or buildings.
kid: You borrow ten sweets to start your lemonade stand and promise to give back two every week until all ten are returned, plus a thank-you sweet.
detail: A term loan provides a lump sum, paid out at once or in instalments, that the borrower repays over an agreed period, usually one to ten years or more, either in regular instalments or at maturity. Interest may be fixed or floating; in India, under RBI rules as of 2025, floating-rate bank loans are linked to the bank's MCLR or an external benchmark such as the repo rate. Companies use term loans to fund capital expenditure, acquisitions or refinancing, and they are typically secured and carry covenants. In leveraged finance, 'Term Loan A' repays steadily and is held by banks, while 'Term Loan B' repays little until maturity and is sold to institutional investors. A common confusion: unlike a revolving credit facility, money repaid on a term loan cannot be borrowed again; once repaid, that part of the facility is gone.
example: Say ABC Ltd takes a ₹10 crore term loan for 5 years at 10% interest, repaying ₹2 crore of principal each year. In year one it pays ₹2 crore of principal plus ₹1 crore of interest; in year two, with ₹8 crore outstanding, it pays ₹2 crore plus ₹80 lakh of interest.

short: A flexible loan limit a company can draw from, repay and draw again as needed, paying interest only on the amount used.
kid: Grandma keeps a jar of ten sweets for you. You can take some when you need them, put them back later, and take them again.
detail: A revolving credit facility gives a borrower access to funds up to a set limit for an agreed period, often three to five years for large companies. The borrower can draw, repay and redraw any amount within the limit, paying interest on what is drawn and a smaller commitment fee on the unused portion. Companies use revolvers as a liquidity backstop and to handle swings in working capital; in India, the closest everyday equivalents are bank cash credit and overdraft facilities. In financial models, the revolver often acts as the balancing item that funds any cash shortfall. Revolvers usually carry financial covenants, and lenders watch for sudden heavy drawdowns, which happened widely in March 2020 as companies rushed to hoard cash. A common confusion: an undrawn revolver is not cash on the balance sheet, and lenders can refuse new drawings if the borrower breaches its covenants.
example: Say ABC Ltd has a ₹200 crore revolver charging 9% on drawn amounts and a 0.5% commitment fee on the undrawn part. If it keeps ₹80 crore drawn all year, it pays ₹7.2 crore of interest plus 0.5% × ₹120 crore = ₹60 lakh in fees.
formula: Annual cost = Drawn amount × Interest rate + Undrawn amount × Commitment fee

short: A short-term loan that covers a funding gap until longer-term money, such as a bond issue or an asset sale, comes in.
kid: You need sweets today for your lemonade stand, but your pocket money only comes on Saturday. A friend lends you some now, and you pay them back on Saturday.
detail: A bridge loan provides temporary financing, usually for a few months to a year, until the borrower secures permanent funding or receives expected cash. It is common in acquisitions: banks commit a bridge facility so the buyer can sign the deal with funding certain, and the bridge is later refinanced through bonds, a term loan, an equity raise or asset sales, known as the takeout. Because it is meant to be short and the takeout carries risk, a bridge loan carries higher interest and fees, which often step up the longer it stays outstanding. In real estate, buyers use bridge loans to purchase a new property before selling the old one. A common confusion: a bridge loan is not cheap short-term money. The real danger is that the planned refinancing fails, for example if bond markets shut, leaving the borrower stuck with expensive debt it cannot easily repay.
example: Say ABC Ltd needs ₹1,000 crore to close an acquisition in January and plans a bond issue in July. It takes a 6-month bridge loan at 10% a year, paying ₹1,000 crore × 10% × 6/12 = ₹50 crore of interest, and repays the principal from the bond proceeds.

short: A large loan provided jointly by a group of lenders under one agreement, with one bank arranging and administering it for all of them.
kid: Your friend needs fifty marbles, but nobody has that many. So five friends each give ten, and one friend keeps track of who gave what.
detail: A syndicated loan is a single loan funded by several banks or institutional investors, each taking a share, so no single lender carries too much exposure to one borrower. A lead arranger structures the deal, negotiates terms and sells portions to other lenders in return for an arrangement fee; an agent bank then handles payments, covenant monitoring and communication with the borrower. Lenders in the syndicate usually rank pari passu and share any security. Syndication lets companies raise very large sums for infrastructure, acquisitions or refinancing through one set of documents. Indian companies use syndicated foreign-currency loans as external commercial borrowings. A common confusion: syndication is not the same as Indian consortium lending. In a consortium, banks lend jointly under a lead bank, with each appraising and sanctioning its own share, while in a syndication an arranger structures the deal and sells it down under one agreement.
example: Say ABC Ltd needs a $500 million loan. Four banks take $100 million each and two more take $50 million each, totalling $500 million, and the arranger earns a 1% fee of $5 million for putting the deal together.
